name: The Heacock household
head: heacock_russel_e

arrival.note: 'Russel E. Heacock, who had come in 1827' - the earliest arrival of any Anglo-American household in this parcel, four years before the town's incorporation and six before the treaty.

party_size_on_arrival.note: Not attested for 1827. What IS attested is the household's size later: a wife and five sons by the spring of 1835.

origin.note: Not attested in anything this project holds.

reason_for_coming.value: Professional and business interests at the settlement
reason_for_coming.note: Andreas states the relation directly in explaining his vote: he lived beyond the proposed town's southern border 'although having his business and professional interests at the settlement'.

lives_at.note: The house he built in the spring of 1835 and moved on rollers. Linked by the inferred-household programme's building parcel (docs/ROADMAP.md K1, phase two); the building record carries the evidence.

works_at.note: NOT MODELLED. He practised law, kept a tavern at Heacock's Point on the South Branch some five miles up, farmed there, and worked as a carpenter. None of the four has a record and the tavern is outside the modelled box.

present_on_scene_date.note: Building a house in the town in the spring of 1835 and advertising as an attorney there on 5 August 1835.

persons.name: Russel E. Heacock

occupation.note: 'Russel E. Heacock, who had come in 1827' - the first of the six lawyers Andreas counts, and a justice of the peace for Cook County who administered the oaths at the incorporation meeting of 5 August 1833. Under date of 5 August 1835 - five weeks after the scene date - Andreas finds him 'advertised as attorney, which is perhaps an indication that he did not seek re-election as a Justice'. He was licensed to keep a tavern at Heacock's Point on the South Branch in April 1831 and cultivated land there, and Judge Goodrich records that 'Heacock in those first years, 1827 to 1835, made more money as a carpenter than as a lawyer or justice'.

persons.note: THE ONE VOTE AGAINST THE TOWN. He cast the single 'against incorporation' ballot on 5 August 1833 - Andreas prints the poll - 'he living at that time beyond the extreme southern border of the proposed town, although having his business and professional interests at the settlement. He moved into the town the following year.' Andreas calls it 'exceptional fidelity to conviction and independence of opinion'. He received one hundred dollars at the Indian treaty of 26 September 1833 and was among the original subscribers to the Chicago Democrat in November 1833.

resident_research.notes: FERGUS 26-29, AS PRINTED: "Heacock, Russel Easton (Old Shallow-Cut, Chicago's first attorney at law), res 129 Adams [died, Summit, Ill., June 20, 1849, aged 70]". The 1843 directory gives the middle name Easton, the trade the 1835 record carries, and a death date and age that put birth about 1779. Research only. Later-volume readings are recorded here and NOT promoted: T-0513 consolidates and T-0514/T-0515 apply.

persons.name: Heacock's wife and children, unnamed

occupation.note: No source records an occupation for this person. This is the ABSENCE of a record rather than a claim that they did no work — the sources of 1835 name the occupations of household heads and almost never those of wives, children or the people counted with them.

persons.note: COUNTED INDIRECTLY AND NOT NAMED. Andreas: he removed in 1834 'that his children might be nearer school', into a house on the east bank of the South Branch a little south of Randolph Street; in the spring of 1835 he built a house on what he supposed was his lot and 'Here his fifth son and youngest child was born'; and in the cholera of 1849 'he fled with his family to a farm he owned at Summit, where he himself, his wife, and two sons were attacked, and died in quick succession'. So the household on 1 July 1835 contains a wife and at least five sons. THE SOURCE COUNTS THEM AND NAMES NONE, so they are one placeholder entry and not seven invented people. Do not count this entry as a person.

research_note: THE OLDEST RESIDENCE, THE ONLY VOTE AGAINST THE TOWN, AND THE LARGEST DOCUMENTED HOUSEHOLD IN THE PARCEL - a wife and five sons, the youngest born in the spring of 1835. It is also the record that best shows why the population layer must precede the building layer: this household of seven had a house built in the season before the scene date, at a street address, which the model does not contain. THE PROJECT SHOULD NOT LOSE THE ROLLERS. A documented instance of a Chicago house being moved bodily one block in 1835 is evidence about construction, weight and the town's attitude to its own buildings, and it belongs in the K4 facades work as much as here.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry.
